books.section: Topic 8.2 The Cold War from 1945 to 1980
Unit 8: The Postwar Period and Cold War (1945-1980)

stimulus.source_note: Original summary passage written for this question; facts from the grounding books.
stimulus.text: In 1972, President Richard Nixon traveled to China, the first visit by an American president to the People's Republic, and to Moscow, where he signed the SALT I agreements limiting nuclear arms. Nixon and his adviser Henry Kissinger called the new approach detente, an easing of tensions with both Communist powers. They hoped to use better relations with each to gain leverage with the other.

source: original; stimulus is an original summary passage written for this question
stem: The SALT I agreements of 1972 are best understood as

options.text: the elimination of all nuclear weapons by both superpowers.
options.misconception: Limits cap growth; elimination would mean zero weapons, which neither side accepted.

options.text: agreed limits on the growth of nuclear arsenals, not disarmament.
a Soviet promise to leave Eastern Europe.
options.misconception: The treaty limited missiles, not Soviet control of Eastern Europe.

options.text: the end of the arms race between the superpowers.
options.misconception: Both sides kept building weapons after 1972, so the race did not end.

rationales.A: Neither side gave up its nuclear weapons in 1972. Both kept thousands of warheads, and the agreements only capped how many launchers each could build.
rationales.B: SALT I froze the number of long-range missile launchers and limited missile defenses. Background from the books: the arsenals stayed huge, but the agreements put a ceiling on their growth for the first time.
rationales.C: SALT I said nothing about Eastern Europe. It was an arms agreement, not a settlement of Europe's borders.
rationales.D: The arms race continued after 1972, with both sides building new kinds of warheads and missiles. SALT I slowed one part of the race rather than ending it.
rationales.general:
1. The passage calls SALT I an agreement limiting nuclear arms, not abolishing them.
2. A limit sets a ceiling: each side may keep what it has and build up to a line, but not past it.
3. That is arms control, not disarmament, and it leaves both arsenals standing.
Remember: Limiting growth and eliminating weapons are different promises; read which one the treaty makes.
